subtopics.title: Flows, Sub-Flows and Flow References
subtopics.meta_description: Learn the key differences between Mule flows and sub-flows, and how the Flow Reference component invokes reusable flow logic in-process without any overhead.
subtopics.summary: Flows typically start with a message source and can handle their own errors, while sub-flows are reusable, source-less logic invoked via Flow Reference.
subtopics.content_html:
Flows are the fundamental organizational unit of Mule application logic, and understanding the distinction between flows, sub-flows, and how Flow Reference connects them is essential before writing any non-trivial integration.

Flows

A flow is a top-level container for a sequence of message processors, typically beginning with a message source (an HTTP Listener, Scheduler, JMS Listener, or similar trigger). A flow can also be triggered indirectly through a Flow Reference from another flow, in which case it doesn't strictly need its own source, though by convention flows with sources represent an entry point into the application.

<flow name="process-order-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/orders" method="POST" />
    <flow-ref name="validate-order-subflow" />
    <flow-ref name="save-order-flow" />
    <logger level="INFO" message="Order #[payload.orderId] processed successfully" />
</flow>

Sub-Flows

A sub-flow is a reusable sequence of processors with no message source and, critically, no error handling of its own—any error raised inside a sub-flow propagates up to the calling flow's error handler. Sub-flows are ideal for extracting common logic (validation, common transformations) that should be reused across multiple flows without duplicating XML.

<sub-flow name="validate-order-subflow">
    <choice>
        <when expression="#[isEmpty(payload.items)]">
            <raise-error type="APP:EMPTY_ORDER" description="Order must contain at least one item" />
        </when>
    </choice>
</sub-flow>

Flows vs. Sub-Flows

AspectFlowSub-Flow
Message sourceUsually has one (HTTP Listener, Scheduler, etc.)Never has one
Error handlingCan define its own error handlerCannot; errors propagate to caller
ExecutionCan run synchronously or asynchronouslyAlways executes synchronously, inline with the caller
Typical useEntry points / top-level orchestrationSmall, reusable logic fragments

Flow Reference

The Flow Reference component invokes another flow or sub-flow by name, passing the current Mule Event to it and receiving back the event resulting from its execution. This is the mechanism that keeps large integrations modular—rather than one enormous flow, logic is decomposed into small, named, testable units.

<flow-ref name="calculate-tax-subflow" doc:name="Calculate Tax" />

Because Flow Reference passes the actual Mule Event (not a copy sent over the network), calling a flow via Flow Reference is efficient—there's no serialization overhead, unlike calling a separate HTTP endpoint. It should not be confused with invoking an entirely separate Mule application; Flow Reference only works within the same running application (or the same domain, if the target flow is in a shared domain project).

Design Guidance

  • Keep individual flows focused on one responsibility—receive a request, orchestrate a few steps, return a response.
  • Extract validation, transformation, or logging logic used in more than one place into sub-flows.
  • Give flows and sub-flows descriptive, consistent names (e.g., get-customer-flow, validate-payload-subflow) so the Flow Reference call sites read clearly.
  • Remember that a sub-flow's errors bubble up—wrap calls to sub-flows in a Try scope within the calling flow if you need localized error handling.
Note: In Mule 4, both flows and sub-flows can technically hold nearly the same processors; the meaningful differences are the presence of a source and independent error handling, not raw capability.

Key Points

  • Flows typically have a message source and can define their own error handling.
  • Sub-flows have no source and always execute synchronously, propagating errors to the caller.
  • Flow Reference invokes another flow/sub-flow in-process, passing the Mule Event directly.

subtopics.title: Mule Event and Message Structure
subtopics.meta_description: Understand the Mule Event structure in Mule 4: payload, attributes, and variables, and how this immutable model powers safe, concurrent flow execution.
subtopics.summary: The immutable Mule Event combines a Message (payload plus attributes) with developer-defined variables that flow through each processor.
subtopics.content_html:
Every message processed by a Mule application is represented internally as a Mule Event. Grasping this data structure is arguably the single most important concept for working effectively with Mule 4, since virtually every expression you write references some part of it.

Anatomy of the Mule Event

A Mule Event is composed of two main parts:

  • Message – the data traveling through the flow, itself split into:
    • payload – the actual body/content of the message (JSON, XML, a Java object, binary data, etc.).
    • attributes – metadata about the payload that varies by connector/source—for HTTP, this includes headers, query parameters, URI parameters, and the HTTP method.
  • Variables – a map of custom key-value data set explicitly in the flow using Set Variable, accessible via vars.variableName and persisting for the life of that flow's processing (subject to scoping rules around async and Flow Reference).

Critically, the Mule Event is immutable: no processor modifies the existing event in place. Instead, each processor (such as Transform Message or Set Payload) produces a brand-new event with an updated payload, while previous state is discarded. This immutability is what makes Mule 4's non-blocking, multi-threaded execution model safe and predictable.

Accessing Event Data with Expressions

<flow name="event-demo-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/customers/{id}" />

    <!-- attributes.uriParams reads the {id} path segment -->
    <set-variable variableName="customerId" value="#[attributes.uriParams.id]" />

    <!-- attributes.headers reads an inbound HTTP header -->
    <set-variable variableName="requestId" value="#[attributes.headers['x-request-id'] default uuid()]" />

    <logger level="INFO" message="Fetching customer #[vars.customerId], requestId=#[vars.requestId]" />

    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  customerId: vars.customerId,
  payloadReceived: payload,
  headers: attributes.headers
}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
</flow>

Payload vs. Attributes vs. Variables

ConceptExpressionTypical Contents
PayloadpayloadThe main body of data being processed (JSON object, XML document, CSV, byte array).
AttributesattributesMetadata from the source connector: HTTP headers, query/URI params, file name, JMS properties.
Variablesvars.nameCustom values explicitly set in the flow to carry state between processors.

Message Metadata: MIME Type

Every payload also carries an associated MIME type (e.g., application/json, application/xml) that DataWeave and connectors use to correctly parse and serialize data. You can inspect or override it with output directives in DataWeave, or the mimeType attribute on Set Payload, ensuring downstream components interpret the data as intended.

Tip: When debugging unexpected behavior, always check whether you're looking at payload versus attributes—a very common beginner mistake is trying to read an HTTP header from payload instead of attributes.headers.

Key Points

  • The Mule Event = Message (payload + attributes) + Variables, and it is immutable end-to-end.
  • Payload is the data; attributes are source-provided metadata; variables are developer-defined state.
  • Every payload carries a MIME type that governs how DataWeave and connectors interpret it.

subtopics.title: Sources and Processors
subtopics.meta_description: Explore Mule flow building blocks: message sources like HTTP Listener and Scheduler, and processor types for transformation, routing, and logging output.
subtopics.summary: Every flow begins with at most one message source, followed by processors that transform, route, call connectors, and log along the way.
subtopics.content_html:
Every Mule flow is built from two categories of components: the message source that triggers the flow, and the message processors that execute in sequence afterward. Understanding the distinction—and the common processor types—is core to reading and writing any Mule flow.

Message Sources

A message source sits at the very beginning of a flow and determines how/when the flow starts executing. Only one message source is allowed per flow (placed as the first element). Common sources include:

  • HTTP Listener – triggers the flow when an HTTP request arrives at a configured path and method.
  • Scheduler – triggers the flow on a fixed frequency or cron expression, useful for batch or polling jobs.
  • JMS Listener / Anypoint MQ Subscriber – triggers when a message arrives on a queue or topic.
  • File / FTP / SFTP Listener – triggers when a new file appears in a watched directory.
  • Database Listener – triggers when new or changed rows match a watermark query.

Message Processors

Everything after the source is a message processor, executed strictly in the order they appear on the canvas/XML. Processors generally fall into a few functional groups:

Transformation Processors

  • Transform Message (DataWeave) – the primary tool for reshaping payload, attributes, or variables.
  • Set Payload / Set Variable – lightweight, single-expression alternatives to a full Transform Message when only a simple assignment is needed.

Flow Control Processors

  • Choice – conditional branching, similar to if/else-if/else.
  • Scatter-Gather – executes multiple routes in parallel and aggregates results.
  • For Each – iterates over a collection, executing nested processors per item.
  • Try – scopes error handling around a subset of processors.

Connector Operations

Connector operations perform the actual work of communicating with external systems—an http:request to call another API, a db:select to query a database, a salesforce:query to run SOQL. These are technically also message processors, just supplied by an installed connector rather than the core module.

Observability Processors

  • Logger – writes a message (often including expressions) to the application log at a chosen level (INFO, DEBUG, WARN, ERROR).
<flow name="poll-and-process-flow">
    <scheduler doc:name="Every 5 minutes">
        <scheduling-strategy>
            <fixed-frequency frequency="5" timeUnit="MINUTES" />
        </scheduling-strategy>
    </scheduler>

    <db:select config-ref="Database_Config" doc:name="Select Pending Orders">
        <db:sql>SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING'</db:sql>
    </db:select>

    <foreach doc:name="For Each Order">
        <http:request config-ref="Fulfillment_API_Config" path="/fulfill" method="POST">
            <http:body>#[payload]</http:body>
        </http:request>
        <logger level="INFO" message="Fulfilled order #[payload.orderId]" />
    </foreach>
</flow>

Sources vs. Processors at a Glance

AspectMessage SourceMessage Processor
PositionAlways first in a flowAnywhere after the source
Count per flowExactly zero or oneZero or many, in sequence
RoleTriggers/starts executionActs on the in-flight Mule Event
Tip: When a flow feels hard to follow, count how many distinct responsibilities its processors cover—more than three or four unrelated steps is usually a sign the logic should be split into sub-flows via Flow Reference.

Key Points

  • A flow has at most one message source, always positioned first.
  • Processors execute strictly top-to-bottom and cover transformation, control flow, connector operations, and logging.
  • Connector operations (HTTP Request, Database Select, etc.) are processors, not sources, when used mid-flow.

subtopics.title: Variables and Payload
subtopics.meta_description: Learn practical patterns for using payload versus variables in Mule 4, including capturing state before transformations overwrite the original payload.
subtopics.summary: Use the payload for the data actively flowing through the application, and variables to preserve values across transformations that replace it.
subtopics.content_html:
Working effectively with Mule 4 means knowing precisely when to use the payload versus a variable, and how to manipulate both cleanly using core components and DataWeave. This article covers the practical patterns developers use every day.

The Payload: Your Primary Data

The payload represents the main content flowing through the application—an incoming JSON request body, a row from a database query, a file's contents. Most processors implicitly operate on the payload; for example, a Transform Message component with no explicit target updates the payload by default.

<set-payload value="#[{ status: 'OK', timestamp: now() }]" doc:name="Set Payload" />

Variables: Carrying State Across Steps

Variables hold values you need to reference later in the flow, after the payload itself has already changed shape one or more times. A very common pattern is capturing an important field before a transformation overwrites the payload:

<flow name="order-total-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/orders" method="POST" />

    <!-- capture the original order id before payload changes shape -->
    <set-variable variableName="originalOrderId" value="#[payload.orderId]" />

    <http:request config-ref="Pricing_API_Config" path="/calculate" method="POST">
        <http:body>#[payload]</http:body>
    </http:request>
    <!-- payload is now the pricing service's response, original data is gone -->

    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  orderId: vars.originalOrderId,
  total: payload.calculatedTotal
}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
</flow>

Without vars.originalOrderId, the order ID from the original request would be lost once the HTTP Request processor replaced the payload with the pricing service's response.

Removing Variables

The Remove Variable component deletes a variable from the event once it's no longer needed, keeping the event lean—particularly useful before returning a response or before an async fork where you don't want unnecessary data copied along.

<remove-variable variableName="originalOrderId" doc:name="Remove Variable" />

Setting Multiple Variables with DataWeave

Within a Transform Message component, switch the target from "Payload" to "Variables" to set several variables at once from a single DataWeave script:

<ee:transform>
    <ee:variables>
        <ee:set-variable variableName="isHighValue"><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/java
---
payload.total > 1000]]></ee:set-variable>
        <ee:set-variable variableName="currency"><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/java
---
payload.currency default "USD"]]></ee:set-variable>
    </ee:variables>
</ee:transform>

Payload vs. Variables: When to Use Each

Use Payload When…Use a Variable When…
Data is actively being transformed and passed to the next processor as "the" main content.You need to preserve a value across one or more transformations that overwrite the payload.
Returning a final response to the caller.Storing flags, IDs, or configuration values used in Choice conditions later in the flow.
Passing data into a connector operation's main input.Accumulating counters or state across a For Each loop iteration.

Common Pitfall: Variable Scope Across Async and Flow Reference

Variables set before an Async scope are copied into the async branch but changes inside the async branch do not propagate back to the main flow, since the async execution continues independently. Similarly, variables set inside a called sub-flow via Flow Reference do propagate back to the caller (because Flow Reference is synchronous and in-process), which is a common source of confusion for developers coming from other integration platforms.

Note: Because the Mule Event is immutable, "setting" a variable technically produces a new event with that variable added/updated—conceptually similar to functional state updates, even though it feels like ordinary imperative assignment in the XML.

Key Points

  • Use the payload for the "current" main data; use variables to preserve values across transformations.
  • Transform Message can target Payload, Variables, or Attributes independently.
  • Remove Variable keeps the event clean once a value is no longer needed.

subtopics.title: Choice Router and Scatter-Gather
subtopics.meta_description: Compare Choice and Scatter-Gather in Mule 4: conditional single-path routing versus parallel fan-out/fan-in execution with aggregated route results returned.
subtopics.summary: Choice executes exactly one matching branch while Scatter-Gather runs multiple routes concurrently and merges their results into one payload.
subtopics.content_html:
Two of the most frequently used flow-control components in Mule 4 are Choice and Scatter-Gather. Both route the Mule Event down different paths, but they solve fundamentally different problems: Choice picks exactly one path based on a condition, while Scatter-Gather runs multiple paths in parallel and combines their results.

Choice Router

Choice evaluates a series of <when> conditions in order and executes the processors nested inside the first one that evaluates to true. If none match, the optional <otherwise> branch executes; if there's no otherwise and no condition matches, Mule raises a MULE:EXPRESSION or routing error.

<flow name="shipping-cost-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/shipping-cost" />
    <choice doc:name="Choice">
        <when expression="#[payload.weightKg > 20]">
            <set-payload value="#[{ cost: 45.00, method: 'Freight' }]" />
        </when>
        <when expression="#[payload.weightKg > 5]">
            <set-payload value="#[{ cost: 15.00, method: 'Ground' }]" />
        </when>
        <otherwise>
            <set-payload value="#[{ cost: 5.00, method: 'Standard' }]" />
        </otherwise>
    </choice>
</flow>

Conditions are written as Mule expressions (DataWeave single-line expressions inside #[ ]), evaluated top to bottom, with only the first matching branch's processors executed—subsequent when blocks are skipped even if they would also evaluate true.

Scatter-Gather

Scatter-Gather executes two or more routes concurrently, each receiving a copy of the same incoming Mule Event, and waits for all routes to complete before aggregating their results into a single outgoing payload—a Java Map keyed by route index (or route name if configured), each value being the result of that route.

<flow name="aggregate-customer-data-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/customers/{id}/summary" />
    <scatter-gather doc:name="Scatter-Gather">
        <route>
            <http:request config-ref="CRM_API_Config" path="/customers/{id}" method="GET">
                <http:uri-params>#[{ id: attributes.uriParams.id }]</http:uri-params>
            </http:request>
        </route>
        <route>
            <http:request config-ref="Billing_API_Config" path="/invoices" method="GET">
                <http:query-params>#[{ customerId: attributes.uriParams.id }]</http:query-params>
            </http:request>
        </route>
    </scatter-gather>

    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  customer: payload."0".payload,
  invoices: payload."1".payload
}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
</flow>

Because routes run in parallel on separate threads from Mule's thread pool, Scatter-Gather is significantly faster than calling the same operations sequentially when they are independent of one another—the total time is roughly the duration of the slowest route rather than the sum of all routes.

Error Behavior

By default, if any route in a Scatter-Gather throws an error, the entire Scatter-Gather fails with a composite routing error (MULE:COMPOSITE_ROUTING) containing details of each route's outcome, rather than silently continuing with partial results. This all-or-nothing behavior should be accounted for with an appropriate error handler when partial failures are acceptable for your use case.

Choice vs. Scatter-Gather

AspectChoiceScatter-Gather
ExecutionExactly one branch runsAll routes run concurrently
Typical use caseConditional business logicAggregating independent calls (fan-out/fan-in)
OutputWhatever the chosen branch producesA map of results keyed by route
Failure handlingOnly the failing branch's error propagatesAny single route failure fails the whole aggregation by default
Tip: Reach for Scatter-Gather when calls are truly independent of one another; if one call's result is needed as input to the next, that's sequential orchestration, not a scatter-gather use case.

Key Points

  • Choice executes exactly one matching branch, evaluated top-to-bottom.
  • Scatter-Gather runs multiple routes in parallel and merges results into a keyed map.
  • Scatter-Gather fails entirely if any single route errors, unless explicitly handled.

subtopics.title: DataWeave vs Mule Expression Language
subtopics.meta_description: Clarify how DataWeave 2.0 replaced Mule Expression Language (MEL) in Mule 4, unifying inline expressions and full transformation scripts into one syntax.
subtopics.summary: DataWeave 2.0 unified Mule 3's separate expression language (MEL) and transformation language into a single syntax used throughout Mule 4.
subtopics.content_html:
Developers new to Mule sometimes encounter references to "Mule Expression Language" (MEL) alongside DataWeave and wonder how they relate. This article clarifies the history and explains why DataWeave 2.0 is the expression and transformation language you should use in all current Mule 4 development.

What Was MEL?

Mule Expression Language was the default expression language in Mule 3, used for lightweight inline expressions such as reading a header (#[message.inboundProperties['header-name']]) or a simple conditional check. It had its own syntax, distinct from the separate transformation language used for heavier data mapping (Mule 3's original DataWeave, introduced later in the Mule 3 lifecycle).

DataWeave 2.0 Unified the Two Roles

With Mule 4, MuleSoft consolidated expression evaluation and data transformation into a single language: DataWeave 2.0. Every #[ ] expression anywhere in a Mule 4 application—inside a Choice condition, a Set Variable value, an HTTP query parameter, or a full Transform Message script—is DataWeave. There is no separate "expression-only" language in Mule 4; MEL is not supported in Mule 4 runtime at all.

<!-- Simple inline DataWeave expression, used exactly like an "expression language" -->
<set-variable variableName="isPremium" value="#[payload.tier == 'GOLD']" />

<choice>
    <when expression="#[vars.isPremium and payload.orderTotal > 500]">
        <set-payload value="#[payload ++ { discount: 0.15 }]" />
    </when>
</choice>

<!-- Full DataWeave script, used exactly like a "transformation language" -->
<ee:transform>
    <ee:message>
        <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map (item) -> {
  sku: item.sku,
  finalPrice: item.price * (1 - (item.discount default 0))
}]]></ee:set-payload>
    </ee:message>
</ee:transform>

Two Syntax Forms, One Language

DataWeave supports both a compact single-line form (used for inline expressions inside attributes like value="#[...]") and the full script form starting with a %dw 2.0 header and an output directive (used inside Transform Message components). Both forms share identical operators, functions, and selector syntax—the only real difference is that a full script can declare variables, functions, and an explicit output MIME type, while an inline expression is a single evaluated expression.

AspectInline Expression (#[ ])Full Script (Transform Message)
LocationXML attributes: value, expression, connector parametersDedicated Transform Message / ee:transform component
HeaderNone needed%dw 2.0 plus output directive
ComplexitySingle expression, no local variable/function declarationsCan define var, fun, multiple named outputs
Typical useConditions, simple value assignment, parameter valuesReshaping payloads between formats/structures

Why This Matters for Learners

Because MEL is obsolete, any tutorial, forum post, or legacy codebase referencing MEL syntax (like message.payload or #[flowVars.x]) is describing Mule 3 patterns that will not work in Mule 4. If you encounter #[flowVars.orderId] in older material, the Mule 4 equivalent is #[vars.orderId]; similarly, Mule 3's message.inboundProperties maps conceptually to Mule 4's attributes.

Note: When migrating a Mule 3 application to Mule 4, MEL expressions must be rewritten in DataWeave 2.0 syntax—this is one of the most common and time-consuming parts of any Mule 3-to-4 migration project.

Key Points

  • Mule Expression Language (MEL) was Mule 3's expression syntax and is not supported in Mule 4.
  • DataWeave 2.0 serves as both the expression language and the transformation language in Mule 4.
  • Inline expressions and full Transform Message scripts share the same underlying DataWeave syntax and semantics.
